compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same delivery, the same four-page document, the same deadline, the same test environment. If one person leads the project and the other is only there to observe, their roles can explain the difference. Each row assumes equal access to the same evidence and the same decision authority.

Every row comes from one situation under the same constraints; the last column names the axis, and either type can use the other column.

| The same item in the same delivery | ENTJ: the basis more likely attended to | ISTP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a team approaching a deadline, either person might keep meetings short or get straight to the work. The deadline and the team’s expectations can explain those behaviours without telling you which type anyone is.

The shared T does account for part of the resemblance: in an argument both readily ask "what is the basis", and neither much accepts "this is how everyone does it". But that alone cannot separate them, because the next question can go in completely different directions.

The difference sits on three preferences: whether attention turns outward or inward more often (E/I); whether sourcing starts from facts and experience or from connections and possibility (S/N); whether outer work settles things first or keeps options (J/P).

### Two kinds of basis in one delivery: commitment and boundary

An outsourced module sits on the table with a smooth demo and a thin document. The same reviewer could check whether the module meets the commitments made to customers and under what conditions it fails. The example illustrates two kinds of evidence, neither of which assigns a type.

The commitment side asks about the chain of responsibility: who guarantees it, when it is delivered, who fixes it when it breaks, how the final payment is tied to remediation. The boundary side asks about the chain of behaviour: what happens under concurrency, what happens when the network drops, what happens when the data volume multiplies by ten. The first decides whether this can be used; the second decides whether it will fail on some late night in use.

Both questions are needed. Watching only commitments may sign off a system that silently drops orders in extreme conditions; watching only boundaries may send back something that needs a few finishing touches, until the supplier wears out and stops improving it. Acceptance problems usually come not from asking the wrong kind of question but from asking only one kind.

Which is asked first is not a criterion. Whoever is responsible for go-live, whatever their type, is more likely to check the schedule and the payment conditions first; whoever has run operations, whatever their type, is more likely to go through the logs and find a reproduction path. Role, authority and deadline override preference.

### Why Ni and Se are shared while every judging function moves

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe.

Start from the outward end. J/P indicates whether a judging or a perceiving process faces the outer world: the J side turns judging outward, the P side turns perceiving outward. E/I then decides whether that outward process lands in the dominant or the auxiliary. ENTJ's outward judging is Te, in the dominant, so the inward perceiving Ni takes the auxiliary; ISTP's outward perceiving is Se, in the auxiliary, so the inward judging Ti takes the dominant. The remaining positions fill in by alternating attitude: Se third and Fi fourth for ENTJ; Ni third and Fe fourth for ISTP.

The result is two names shared and two different, none of them in the same place: Ni and Se are still present in both, with auxiliary and third swapped; and the judging end has nothing in common — Te and Fi for ENTJ, Ti and Fe for ISTP, no overlap at any of the four judging positions. This is not the same as "Fi and Ti swapping".

That explains a familiar scene: the two reach the same conclusion on a technical judgement and their reasons will not connect. But sharing Ni and Se only means each has a set of perceiving processes; it does not follow that they notice the same clues, or which line of work each is good at — what you see depends on how much information you have, which stage you stand at, and who asked you.

Whether the third position is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: ENTJ's Se and ISTP's Ni are labelled in different ways. When you meet another version, check whether it cites a source, then read the first two positions for this pair; the disagreement does not affect the first two and does not explain how early anyone moves. Both base descriptions are the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the three passages below are editorial composites, used to see which kind of basis each might cite, not to allocate roles, responsibility or management style by type.

When the two run an acceptance together, the usual arrangement gives contract terms and timing to whoever knows the contract better, and technical review to whoever knows the system better, with one rule both accept: no signature until the technical review passes, and none until the terms are written. The arrangement follows experience and available time, not type; the same type can perfectly well do the reverse.

### Accepting outsourced development: both kinds of basis on paper

(Fictional scene.) A supplier delivers an order-sync module, the demo scrolls rows of data past, the document runs to four pages, and the contract says final payment within thirty days of acceptance. The module has to be integrated for next month's promotion, and a week's delay misses it.

One person may focus on schedule and terms: whether the interface documentation is complete, who handles exceptions, whether final payment can be tied to an observation period, and whether the acceptance form states a remediation deadline. The other may focus on behavioural boundaries: pull the module into their own environment, load last year's historical orders through it, and find that a bulk import above two thousand rows silently skips some records without raising an error.

Both findings have to go on paper, and a formal acceptance record should carry the technical defect and the contractual responsibility together. The defect side states the trigger conditions, the scope of impact, the owner, the remediation deadline and the conditions for re-verification; the terms side states the payment conditions, the observation period, incident response and dispute handling. Record only one and the other half surfaces after signature — if the technology was not verified, an exception becomes "you don't know how to use it"; if the terms were not written, the fix is done and nobody owns it.

On "can demo" and "can reproduce": a smooth demo does not show it will be smooth on your data, so it is worth agreeing the delivery version, the runtime environment, the test data, the expected result and how evidence is kept, and asking them to run it in your environment on your data. But failing to reproduce does not mean the supplier does not understand their own code — it may be an environment difference, different data or a version mismatch, and the conditions should be checked further rather than a conclusion drawn.

Record in three layers: "observed", "reliably reproduced", "cause identified". Mixing the three in one sentence makes accountability impossible afterwards. Test thresholds — data volume, concurrency, network-drop duration — follow the contract and the actual load, not numbers borrowed from elsewhere.

Severe issues and deferrable items are handled separately. Something that threatens an outward commitment, such as a suspected silent drop, is remediated and re-verified before any signature is discussed; something deferrable, such as layout or wording, goes into the observation period as agreed. Applying "any single failure goes into the observation period" to everything merges blocking defects with finishing work.

### A cousin comes for a summer internship: real work or not

(Fictional scene.) A cousin joins the team as a summer intern. One person proposes a small hands-on task from the start. Another proposes a period of observation so the intern understands the system first. Both weigh the same time and risk constraints, and either preference could inform either proposal.

The first is counting time: the internship is only six weeks, and two weeks of watching without touching is a waste. The second is counting something else: an intern who has not understood the data structures yet can break something that takes two days to roll back, and will not know what they changed.

This is not about who is more willing to mentor. The first worries the opportunity is wasted; the second worries damage is being planted. A middle path: in week one give a small module that can break without affecting the main flow, expand the assignment when the intern is ready, using approved test data, and before every commit write three lines — what changed, why, and how it was verified.

Counterexamples are common too: some ENTJs will patiently mentor an intern for three months, hands on; some ISTPs will drop a newcomer into the hardest pit because that is how they learned. How someone mentors depends on their own mentoring experience, the risk in the task, the intern's readiness and the team's staffing at the time, with no correspondence to type.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first thing taken as evidence is "who understands the technology better". Both may know more than the other in one field, and both will ask very basic questions in an unfamiliar one. Technical depth is experience, not preference.

The second is separating them by behaviour under pressure. Being rushed or calm depends on the information available, authority, sleep and whether anyone nearby can take over, and both types supply plenty of counterexamples: an ISTP interrupted repeatedly will snap, and an ENTJ who has carried an incident alone can go frighteningly quiet. Listing such counterexamples only shows the behaviour is unstable; it does not prove that "one type is quicker to snap", so those summaries should not be used in the first place.

The third is reading a function position as a sequence of actions. The dominant function is not "the first thing done", and the auxiliary is not "the second". A function is a processing position in the model; which step comes first is decided by the task, the duty and the amount of information.

The fourth is treating a checklist division as an exclusive task. Writing the terms and running the reproduction belong to no type; who drafts which part follows experience and authority, and after merging, both parts should have been read by someone.

(Fictional scene.) A supplier delivers an order-sync module, the demo scrolls rows of data past, the document runs to four pages, and the contract says final payment within thirty days of acceptance. The module has to be integrated for next month's promotion, and a week's delay misses it.

One person may focus on schedule and terms: whether the interface documentation is complete, who handles exceptions, whether final payment can be tied to an observation period, and whether the acceptance form states a remediation deadline. The other may focus on behavioural boundaries: pull the module into their own environment, load last year's historical orders through it, and find that a bulk import above two thousand rows silently skips some records without raising an error.

Both findings have to go on paper, and a formal acceptance record should carry the technical defect and the contractual responsibility together. The defect side states the trigger conditions, the scope of impact, the owner, the remediation deadline and the conditions for re-verification; the terms side states the payment conditions, the observation period, incident response and dispute handling. Record only one and the other half surfaces after signature — if the technology was not verified, an exception becomes "you don't know how to use it"; if the terms were not written, the fix is done and nobody owns it.

On "can demo" and "can reproduce": a smooth demo does not show it will be smooth on your data, so it is worth agreeing the delivery version, the runtime environment, the test data, the expected result and how evidence is kept, and asking them to run it in your environment on your data. Record in three layers: "observed", "reliably reproduced", "cause identified". Mixing the three in one sentence makes accountability impossible afterwards. Test thresholds — data volume, concurrency, network-drop duration — follow the contract and the actual load, not numbers borrowed from elsewhere.

Severe issues and deferrable items are handled separately. Something that threatens an outward commitment, such as a suspected silent drop, is remediated and re-verified before any signature is discussed; something deferrable, such as layout or wording, goes into the observation period as agreed. body: In a team approaching a deadline, either person might keep meetings short or get straight to the work. The deadline and the team’s expectations can explain those behaviours without telling you which type anyone is.

The shared T does account for part of the resemblance: in an argument both readily ask "what is the basis", and neither much accepts "this is how everyone does it". But that alone cannot separate them, because the next question can go in completely different directions.

The difference sits on three preferences: whether attention turns outward or inward more often (E/I); whether sourcing starts from facts and experience or from connections and possibility (S/N); whether outer work settles things first or keeps options (J/P).
### Two kinds of basis in one delivery: commitment and boundary

An outsourced module sits on the table with a smooth demo and a thin document. The same reviewer could check whether the module meets the commitments made to customers and under what conditions it fails. The example illustrates two kinds of evidence, neither of which assigns a type.

The commitment side asks about the chain of responsibility: who guarantees it, when it is delivered, who fixes it when it breaks, how the final payment is tied to remediation. The boundary side asks about the chain of behaviour: what happens under concurrency, what happens when the network drops, what happens when the data volume multiplies by ten. The first decides whether this can be used; the second decides whether it will fail on some late night in use.

Both questions are needed. Watching only commitments may sign off a system that silently drops orders in extreme conditions; watching only boundaries may send back something that needs a few finishing touches, until the supplier wears out and stops improving it. Acceptance problems usually come not from asking the wrong kind of question but from asking only one kind.

Which is asked first is not a criterion. Whoever is responsible for go-live, whatever their type, is more likely to check the schedule and the payment conditions first; whoever has run operations, whatever their type, is more likely to go through the logs and find a reproduction path. Role, authority and deadline override preference.
### Why Ni and Se are shared while every judging function moves
In the common four-function notation used here, ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe.

Start from the outward end. J/P indicates whether a judging or a perceiving process faces the outer world: the J side turns judging outward, the P side turns perceiving outward. E/I then decides whether that outward process lands in the dominant or the auxiliary. ENTJ's outward judging is Te, in the dominant, so the inward perceiving Ni takes the auxiliary; ISTP's outward perceiving is Se, in the auxiliary, so the inward judging Ti takes the dominant. The remaining positions fill in by alternating attitude: Se third and Fi fourth for ENTJ; Ni third and Fe fourth for ISTP.

The result is two names shared and two different, none of them in the same place: Ni and Se are still present in both, with auxiliary and third swapped; and the judging end has nothing in common — Te and Fi for ENTJ, Ti and Fe for ISTP, no overlap at any of the four judging positions. This is not the same as "Fi and Ti swapping".

That explains a familiar scene: the two reach the same conclusion on a technical judgement and their reasons will not connect. But sharing Ni and Se only means each has a set of perceiving processes; it does not follow that they notice the same clues, or which line of work each is good at — what you see depends on how much information you have, which stage you stand at, and who asked you.

Whether the third position is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: ENTJ's Se and ISTP's Ni are labelled in different ways. When you meet another version, check whether it cites a source, then read the first two positions for this pair; the disagreement does not affect the first two and does not explain how early anyone moves. Both base descriptions are the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).

comparison_public_projection_v1.summary:
ENTJ and ISTP share only T, and differ on E/I, S/N and J/P. Each difference has its own meaning and none can be flattened into "one wants results, one wants logic".

- E/I: the ENTJ side, E, turns attention and energy more naturally toward the outer world — people, schedules, commitments made outward; the ISTP side, I, turns more naturally inward — their own reasoning and judgement. This is about where attention and energy tend to go. Either person may sit quietly through an entire meeting.
- S/N: ENTJ's Intuition (N) emphasises connections, patterns and possibilities. ISTP's Sensing (S) emphasises observable facts and experience — what actually happened in a run, the steps in the document, this set of parameters in hand.
- T/F: both have T, meaning judgement leans toward logical criteria that can be applied consistently. The Feeling preference gives more weight to values and how decisions affect people. Sharing this only means both readily ask "what is the basis"; it does not say which end the basis sits on.
- J/P: the ENTJ side, J, more often settles arrangements, conclusions and responsibility when facing the outer world; the ISTP side, P, more often keeps options until new information arrives.

Using the type-dynamics convention on this page, the stacks are: Te–Ni–Se–Fi for ENTJ and Ti–Se–Ni–Fe for ISTP. Both list Ni and Se, with auxiliary and third swapped — ENTJ has Ni auxiliary and Se third, ISTP has Se auxiliary and Ni third; the judging functions are Te and Fi for ENTJ and Ti and Fe for ISTP, with no overlap at any of the four judging positions. The attitude of the third process is labelled differently elsewhere, and this arrangement is a convention adopted here, not the Foundation's only version.

These describe emphasis inside the model. They do not predict who asks what first, who is better suited to acceptance testing, or whether two people work well together. In the same acceptance review, either may run it first or ask about the schedule first; order depends more on duty, authority, experience and deadline.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a team approaching a deadline, either person might keep meetings short or get straight to the work. The deadline and the team’s expectations can explain those behaviours without telling you which type anyone is.

The shared T does account for part of the resemblance: in an argument both readily ask "what is the basis", and neither much accepts "this is how everyone does it". But that alone cannot separate them, because the next question can go in completely different directions.

The difference sits on three preferences: whether attention turns outward or inward more often (E/I); whether sourcing starts from facts and experience or from connections and possibility (S/N); whether outer work settles things first or keeps options (J/P).

### Two kinds of basis in one delivery: commitment and boundary

An outsourced module sits on the table with a smooth demo and a thin document. The same reviewer could check whether the module meets the commitments made to customers and under what conditions it fails. The example illustrates two kinds of evidence, neither of which assigns a type.

The commitment side asks about the chain of responsibility: who guarantees it, when it is delivered, who fixes it when it breaks, how the final payment is tied to remediation. The boundary side asks about the chain of behaviour: what happens under concurrency, what happens when the network drops, what happens when the data volume multiplies by ten. The first decides whether this can be used; the second decides whether it will fail on some late night in use.

Both questions are needed. Watching only commitments may sign off a system that silently drops orders in extreme conditions; watching only boundaries may send back something that needs a few finishing touches, until the supplier wears out and stops improving it. Acceptance problems usually come not from asking the wrong kind of question but from asking only one kind.

Which is asked first is not a criterion. Whoever is responsible for go-live, whatever their type, is more likely to check the schedule and the payment conditions first; whoever has run operations, whatever their type, is more likely to go through the logs and find a reproduction path. Role, authority and deadline override preference.

### Why Ni and Se are shared while every judging function moves

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi and ISTP is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe.

Start from the outward end. J/P indicates whether a judging or a perceiving process faces the outer world: the J side turns judging outward, the P side turns perceiving outward. E/I then decides whether that outward process lands in the dominant or the auxiliary. ENTJ's outward judging is Te, in the dominant, so the inward perceiving Ni takes the auxiliary; ISTP's outward perceiving is Se, in the auxiliary, so the inward judging Ti takes the dominant. The remaining positions fill in by alternating attitude: Se third and Fi fourth for ENTJ; Ni third and Fe fourth for ISTP.

The result is two names shared and two different, none of them in the same place: Ni and Se are still present in both, with auxiliary and third swapped; and the judging end has nothing in common — Te and Fi for ENTJ, Ti and Fe for ISTP, no overlap at any of the four judging positions. This is not the same as "Fi and Ti swapping".

That explains a familiar scene: the two reach the same conclusion on a technical judgement and their reasons will not connect. But sharing Ni and Se only means each has a set of perceiving processes; it does not follow that they notice the same clues, or which line of work each is good at — what you see depends on how much information you have, which stage you stand at, and who asked you.

Whether the third position is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: ENTJ's Se and ISTP's Ni are labelled in different ways. When you meet another version, check whether it cites a source, then read the first two positions for this pair; the disagreement does not affect the first two and does not explain how early anyone moves. Both base descriptions are the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp).

sections.body_md:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same delivery, the same four-page document, the same deadline, the same test environment. If one person leads the project and the other is only there to observe, their roles can explain the difference. Each row assumes equal access to the same evidence and the same decision authority.

Every row comes from one situation under the same constraints; the last column names the axis, and either type can use the other column.

| The same item in the same delivery | ENTJ: the basis more likely attended to | ISTP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The first thing to confirm after receiving the module | Whether it can be integrated before next month's promotion, and who carries a one-week delay | Whether the steps in the document can be run through, and where they stall | Two checks — delivery and trial use — both depending on duty and evidence |
| When the demo runs smoothly | Which patterns in the same demo suggest that it might behave differently at higher order volumes | Which inputs and volumes were actually tested, and what the observed results were | Sourcing preference, leaning S/N |
| An intermittent error appears | Agree on a provisional plan for the follow-up under the same acceptance criteria | Keep several follow-up arrangements open while both examine how to reproduce the error | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| The supplier says "this is standard in the industry" | Whether that sentence can go into a contract annex, and who delivers on it | Demonstrate it here and now, and see whether the behaviour reproduces | Both can demand a verifiable demo and pin down commitment and responsibility |
| The threshold before signing | Check the documented milestones and responsibilities against the agreed criteria | Check the observed behaviour against those same agreed criteria | Basis for judgement, the shared T, differing in where it lands |
| What to watch in the first week after go-live | Set a provisional on-call schedule within the agreed response requirements | Keep feasible on-call arrangements open while the same log is reviewed | Outward stance, leaning J/P |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. The same person switches sides: an ISTP responsible for go-live will check the schedule and payment terms before signing, because that is the duty; an ENTJ who sees a suspected silent order drop will demand a reproduction first, because that risk destroys an outward commitment. An ENTJ with years of supplier-side delivery may know the documents and reproduction paths better than an ISTP. Role, authority, deadline and experience all rewrite the two columns.

Scope note: the three passages below are editorial composites, used to see which kind of basis each might cite, not to allocate roles, responsibility or management style by type.

When the two run an acceptance together, the usual arrangement gives contract terms and timing to whoever knows the contract better, and technical review to whoever knows the system better, with one rule both accept: no signature until the technical review passes, and none until the terms are written. The arrangement follows experience and available time, not type; the same type can perfectly well do the reverse.

### Accepting outsourced development: both kinds of basis on paper

(Fictional scene.) A supplier delivers an order-sync module, the demo scrolls rows of data past, the document runs to four pages, and the contract says final payment within thirty days of acceptance. The module has to be integrated for next month's promotion, and a week's delay misses it.

One person may focus on schedule and terms: whether the interface documentation is complete, who handles exceptions, whether final payment can be tied to an observation period, and whether the acceptance form states a remediation deadline. The other may focus on behavioural boundaries: pull the module into their own environment, load last year's historical orders through it, and find that a bulk import above two thousand rows silently skips some records without raising an error.

Both findings have to go on paper, and a formal acceptance record should carry the technical defect and the contractual responsibility together. The defect side states the trigger conditions, the scope of impact, the owner, the remediation deadline and the conditions for re-verification; the terms side states the payment conditions, the observation period, incident response and dispute handling. Record only one and the other half surfaces after signature — if the technology was not verified, an exception becomes "you don't know how to use it"; if the terms were not written, the fix is done and nobody owns it.

On "can demo" and "can reproduce": a smooth demo does not show it will be smooth on your data, so it is worth agreeing the delivery version, the runtime environment, the test data, the expected result and how evidence is kept, and asking them to run it in your environment on your data. But failing to reproduce does not mean the supplier does not understand their own code — it may be an environment difference, different data or a version mismatch, and the conditions should be checked further rather than a conclusion drawn.

Record in three layers: "observed", "reliably reproduced", "cause identified". Mixing the three in one sentence makes accountability impossible afterwards. Test thresholds — data volume, concurrency, network-drop duration — follow the contract and the actual load, not numbers borrowed from elsewhere.

Severe issues and deferrable items are handled separately. Something that threatens an outward commitment, such as a suspected silent drop, is remediated and re-verified before any signature is discussed; something deferrable, such as layout or wording, goes into the observation period as agreed. Applying "any single failure goes into the observation period" to everything merges blocking defects with finishing work.

### A cousin comes for a summer internship: real work or not

(Fictional scene.) A cousin joins the team as a summer intern. One person proposes a small hands-on task from the start. Another proposes a period of observation so the intern understands the system first. Both weigh the same time and risk constraints, and either preference could inform either proposal.

The first is counting time: the internship is only six weeks, and two weeks of watching without touching is a waste. The second is counting something else: an intern who has not understood the data structures yet can break something that takes two days to roll back, and will not know what they changed.

This is not about who is more willing to mentor. The first worries the opportunity is wasted; the second worries damage is being planted. A middle path: in week one give a small module that can break without affecting the main flow, expand the assignment when the intern is ready, using approved test data, and before every commit write three lines — what changed, why, and how it was verified.

Counterexamples are common too: some ENTJs will patiently mentor an intern for three months, hands on; some ISTPs will drop a newcomer into the hardest pit because that is how they learned. How someone mentors depends on their own mentoring experience, the risk in the task, the intern's readiness and the team's staffing at the time, with no correspondence to type.

sections.body_md:
The first thing taken as evidence is "who understands the technology better". Both may know more than the other in one field, and both will ask very basic questions in an unfamiliar one. Technical depth is experience, not preference.

The second is separating them by behaviour under pressure. Being rushed or calm depends on the information available, authority, sleep and whether anyone nearby can take over, and both types supply plenty of counterexamples: an ISTP interrupted repeatedly will snap, and an ENTJ who has carried an incident alone can go frighteningly quiet. Listing such counterexamples only shows the behaviour is unstable; it does not prove that "one type is quicker to snap", so those summaries should not be used in the first place.

The third is reading a function position as a sequence of actions. The dominant function is not "the first thing done", and the auxiliary is not "the second". A function is a processing position in the model; which step comes first is decided by the task, the duty and the amount of information.

The fourth is treating a checklist division as an exclusive task. Writing the terms and running the reproduction belong to no type; who drafts which part follows experience and authority, and after merging, both parts should have been read by someone.

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the assessment name, version, language and scoring convention first, then the conditions you answered from: was a project in progress, what role were you carrying, how much pressure, and what did you read the items to mean. All of these push answers to one side, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency.

The practice does not need to score the order of actions. Pick a few recent comparable matters — an acceptance, a scheduling meeting, a discussion with flatmates about replacing an appliance — and write three lines each: your role and constraints, which information you trusted, which standard you weighed, and whether you settled it outward or kept it open. If the same kind of basis recurs across several, it is worth discussing as your habit in sourcing and judging; it is not a typing rule and is not scored.

Nor should you define yourself by familiarity, calmness or one performance. The default response in a familiar field, the tension in an unfamiliar task, one unusually steady moment — all are the conditions of the time at work. If the item bank reports dimension scores, look at which sit nearer the boundary; sitting near a boundary only means that item is sensitive to changes in your answers, not that two complete types both hold.

No. The two share T, and both lean toward impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently; asking "what is the basis" is a shared trait in this pair, not a distinction.

To explore the differences, look separately at where attention goes (E/I), which information gets more weight (S/N) and whether the person prefers to settle an outward plan or keep options open (J/P). Compare situations in which they had similar responsibilities and room to choose. A single question or speaking style cannot identify a type.
items.question: Both like to ask for the basis — can that alone separate them?

items.answer:
It means only two perceiving process names are shared, and their positions are swapped; the judging end has no overlap — ENTJ has Te dominant and Fi inferior, ISTP has Ti dominant and Fe inferior.

What follows is that the two enter a matter with different emphases. What does not follow is that they see the same clues, who is better at the technology, or who is better suited to acceptance. Given the same record, one may stress checkable acceptance criteria and where responsibility lands, the other whether the behaviour reproduces and whether the explanation holds; both can check logic and both can look at results.
items.question: They share Ni and Se while all four judging positions differ — what does that mean?

items.answer:
Not by who sets the goal first. The order of goal and means can go either way in either person; anyone handed a clear target, of any type, will pick up the target first.

Ask which information shaped the goal: concrete observations and prior experience, or patterns and possibilities beyond the immediate task. Either person can use both, and the order in which they speak or set the goal offers no basis for assigning a type.
items.question: ISTP also sets goals and ENTJ also takes things apart — how do you not mix them up?

Length depends on the deliverable and the contract, not on type; the two lists also overlap heavily, because interface, performance and exception handling are written by both.

items.question: Accepting the same outsourced delivery, whose checklist is longer?

items.answer:
By experience, authority, time and what each person actually wants to do — not by "who is more diligent" or "who is more like a type".

Renting together, for instance: whoever knows contracts handles the lease, the deposit and the landlord; whoever prefers hands-on work handles utilities, the network and appliance repairs. In another pair of flatmates the division may be exactly reversed. If you swap, say for how long and who handles problems; the division exists to reduce repeated coordination, not to label anyone.
